Redeem it anonymously with an attacker-generated ed25519 public key:

GET /setup?public-key=q2UkizMX0Go4mHwW2BXepqkzpP5FHlagEft8M32t0EM%3D HTTP/1.1 Host: localhost:9883 Accept: application/ad+json Response 200 OK returns a Redirect confirming the new agent:

Unauthenticated write to the entire Drive: read/modify/delete any resource, create/alter Agents, reconfigure permissions. This is a complete takeover on a fresh deployment. items.detail:
Vulnérabilité critique CVE-2026-130001 affectant mustache (rubygems) (score CVSS 9.8).

Mustache for Ruby: RCE using built-in method access

The vulnerability was fully disclosed to the maintainer in private prior to security advisories were enabled for the project. This advisory presents a limited information for initial release to provide a time window for installing updates. Full information with PoCs would be added later.

Mustache template engine for Ruby in versions 1.1.2 and earlier allows remote attackers to achieve arbitrary code execution through accessing specific built-in methods in an attacker-supplied template.

Mustache is often suggested as a safe simple template language to avoid SSTI vulnerabilities. 1 2

Mustache for Ruby up to version 1.1.2 did not properly restrict method access which allowed chaining multiple built-in methods to achieve arbitrary code execution.

Successful exploitation of this vulnerability does not depend on any configuration or objects passed to the template engine. An attacker controlling the template string can achieve arbitrary code execution without any additional requirements.

Additional methods provided by the application or installed gems can further expand the attack surface but exploitation was proven without them.

Incident de sécurité rapporté par Global Sec Mag.

Norwegian Gas Giant Equinor confirms cyberattack on IT systems, with no impact on production or confirmed data theft. Equinor, Europe’s largest gas supplier, said on 17 November it had detected an ongoing cyberattack against some IT systems. The Norwegian company said the attack had not affected operations and production, and it had taken steps to neutralise it. “Equinor has detected an ongoing cyber-attack against certain IT systems. Relevant resources have been mobilised to neutralise the attack and regain full integrity.” reads the statement published by the company. “As this is not a virus attack, there is no risk of the attack spreading. At present, there is no indication that the attack has consequences for employees, partners or suppliers. Production remains unaffected.” The energy giant said there was also no indication data had been stolen. A company spokesperson declined to give further details. The disruption reached everyday work, not the wells. Norwegian news agency NTB reported, citing the company, that IT applications and internal systems were affected, and a person at Equinor told Reuters the internal email system was down. items.detail:
Incident de sécurité rapporté par The Record.

A bipartisan Senate duo urged the White House to launch a national effort to more robustly confront AI-enabled cyber threats in light of recent security incidents involving artificial intelligence.

Two leading members of the Senate urged the White House on Tuesday to launch a national effort to more robustly confront AI-enabled cyber threats in light of recent security incidents involving artificial intelligence.

In a letter to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, Sens. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) and Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) warned that AI is “rapidly increasing the ability to discover and exploit weaknesses in software” and that the country’s defenses “are not keeping pace.”

“The fundamental problem is that AI can discover software weaknesses and help attackers exploit them faster than many organizations can respond,” the senators said. “Even when fixes are available, testing and installing patches across interconnected systems can take weeks or months, potentially disrupting essential services.”

The letter cites recent incidents where AI was used to discover obscure bugs and power cyber intrusions in Japan . The senators also raised concerns from banks about AI agents, which are increasingly accessing bank accounts. Several U.S. banks have said they are unable to tell whether AI agents are rogue or are accessing data on behalf of customers.

Chinese-developed AI models are also being used widely for a variety of nefarious purposes, the lawmakers said.

Rounds is the chairman of the Senate Armed Services subcommittee on cybersecurity and has repeatedly called on the White House to do more to confront risks posed by AI.

Signal de veille — The Record.

Google can take possession of defunct Spirit Airlines' data for $10 million, a federal bankruptcy judge has ruled. The tech giant agreed to protections as it plans to use the data in AI projects.

A New York federal bankruptcy judge on Tuesday greenlit the sale of Spirit Airlines’ employees’ data to Google, a decision that follows the tech giant’s agreement to abide by restrictions on how it uses and deidentifies the information.

Soon after the outcry began, Google agreed to new terms designed to better protect sensitive data.

On November 9, the union withdrew its objection to the sale, citing Google’s pledge to exclude employees’ health and medical data, alcohol and drug testing results, safety and disciplinary records and identification documents. The tech giant also agreed to what the union called a “rigorous de-identification process” and a mandatory review of the deidentified data by an independent assessor chosen in collaboration with the union.

In signing off on the sale, U.S. Bankruptcy Judge Sean Lane said the “procedures for the deidentification, transformation and preparation of the data” comply with applicable data protection laws, according to a court filing .

The company has said it intends to use the data for AI model training. The agreement is the first of this scale to emerge in the AI era. The dataset includes an estimated 100 million emails and half-billion Microsoft Teams messages, which experts say will be useful for training agents handling professional tasks.

While the flight attendants’ union has celebrated the protections it won, Arjun Bhatnagar, the CEO of the consumer privacy startup Cloaked, said the data sale still poses a threat to employees.

Signal de veille — The Record.

Day 2 of the NSA Net's disruptions included staggered arrivals and logins at Fort Meade, while a source said classified national security work continued unimpeded.

Disruptions at the National Security Agency entered their second day on Wednesday as the spy organization worked to get its internal communications network back up and fully running.

The system, known as NSA Net, experienced intermittent outages on Tuesday, leading the agency to tell its work force to stagger arrivals at its headquarters at Fort Meade, Maryland. It eventually closed its campus to most employees by the evening, according to sources.

Non-essential personnel were sent a "Code Gray" notification late Tuesday night, informing them to arrive at 10 a.m. Wednesday. However, that time has already been moved to the afternoon and could change again, said a source familiar with the ongoing situation.

Meanwhile, the agency’s cafeteria, and a Starbucks located on its campus, remain closed.

The same person said the network is working but NSA leaders are still staggering personnel because the login process is the most taxing process on the system.

They also said comments made Tuesday by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton — that the outage was due to maintenance affecting PHP, a common programming language — were correct.

Signal de veille — Infosecurity Mag.

National Audit Office report warns that risk management failures lead to poor government decisions

The number of chief risk officers (CROs) in UK government has more than doubled over the past decade, but most industry professionals working in Whitehall believe they lack influence, according to a new National Audit Office (NAO) report.

The spending watchdog published its report, Risk management in government: improving capability and decision making , on November 18.

It noted that effective risk management is important in helping to manage fast emerging risks, like the recent PHP vulnerabilities , which have the potential to disrupt public services and lead to costly recovery work.

It can also “help public bodies make better decisions, adapt to uncertainty and take well-managed risks to innovate and improve services,” the NAO argued.

However, 58% of risk professionals it polled claimed they are typically brought in too late to shape decisions.

“We found limited evidence of major decisions or organizational direction changing because of input from risk professionals,” the report noted. “In hierarchical organizations, the often low seniority of those leading risk teams can also restrict their access to senior decision-making forums.”
